Keywords: BaseModel create update response schema separation Pydantic v2 ConfigDict
Description: Define separate Pydantic models for Create (input without id/timestamps) Update (all Optional fields) and Response (output with computed fields). Never reuse one model for all operations. Use model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True) on response models for ORM compatibility.
When to Use: For every resource endpoint where input and output shapes differ
Code Example:
"from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic import ConfigDict

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: str
    password: str

class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    email: str | None = None
    full_name: str | None = None

class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    email: str
    full_name: str | None = None
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)"
Anti-Pattern: Using a single User model for request body DB model and response — leaks hashed passwords internal fields

Keywords: from_attributes ORM mode SQLAlchemy ConfigDict model_config response
Description: Enable from_attributes=True in model_config to allow Pydantic to read data from ORM object attributes directly. This is the Pydantic v2 replacement for the deprecated class Config: orm_mode = True.
When to Use: When your response_model needs to serialize SQLAlchemy ORM instances
Code Example:
"from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    email: str
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

# Now works with SQLAlchemy rows:
user_orm = db.get(User, user_id)
return UserResponse.model_validate(user_orm)"
Anti-Pattern: Using deprecated class Config: orm_mode = True (Pydantic v1 style) — raises deprecation warnings in v2

Keywords: field_validator classmethod validator custom validation Pydantic v2
Description: Use @field_validator to apply custom validation logic to individual fields. Must be a classmethod. Can validate and transform values. Use mode='before' to run before type coercion.
When to Use: When built-in constraints (min_length ge le) are not sufficient for the field
Anti-Pattern: Validating request data inside route handlers with if-statements — not reusable and bypasses OpenAPI

Keywords: model_validator mode after root cross field multi-field constraint
Description: Use @model_validator(mode='after') for validation that depends on multiple fields simultaneously. The validator receives the fully constructed model instance.
When to Use: When one field's validity depends on another (e.g. password confirmation range validation)
Anti-Pattern: Doing multi-field validation inside route handlers with manual if/raise

Keywords: Annotated Field ge le min_length max_length pattern gt lt Query Path Body
Description: Use Annotated with Field() to declare constraints declaratively on Pydantic fields. The same Annotated pattern also works directly for FastAPI Query Path and Body parameters.
When to Use: When you need to constrain numeric ranges string lengths or regex patterns on model fields or path/query params
Code Example:
"from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from fastapi import Query

class CreateItem(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)]
    price: Annotated[float, Field(gt=0)]
    quantity: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=9999)]

@router.get('/items')
async def list_items(
    skip: Annotated[int, Query(ge=0)] = 0,
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10,
): ..."
Anti-Pattern: Validating numeric ranges with if-statements in the route body — not reflected in OpenAPI schema

Keywords: nested model composition embedded sub-object relationship
Description: Compose complex schemas by embedding Pydantic models inside other models. FastAPI generates fully nested OpenAPI schemas. Works with from_attributes=True for ORM relationships.
When to Use: When a resource has sub-objects (User with Address Post with Author)
Code Example:
"from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class AddressResponse(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    email: str
    address: AddressResponse | None = None
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)"
Anti-Pattern: Flattening nested objects into one model with name-prefixed fields (e.g. address_street) — poor API design

Description: Use response_model_exclude or response_model_include on path operations to filter specific fields from an existing response model without creating a new schema.
When to Use: When you want to reuse a response model but omit specific fields (e.g. return User without email on a public endpoint)
Code Example:
"@router.get(
    '/{user_id}/public',
    response_model=UserResponse,
    response_model_exclude={'email', 'hashed_password'},
)
async def get_public_user(user_id: int, db: DbSession): ..."
Anti-Pattern: Use sparingly — creating dedicated response schemas is usually cleaner. response_model_exclude is missing from OpenAPI so the excluded fields still appear in docs.

Keywords: pydantic_settings BaseSettings env environment variables config lru_cache
Description: Use pydantic-settings BaseSettings to read configuration from environment variables with type validation. Combine with @lru_cache so settings are loaded once. Supports .env files via env_file.
When to Use: Loading typed configuration from environment variables in FastAPI apps
Anti-Pattern: Reading os.environ directly in handlers — no type validation no IDE autocomplete no OpenAPI integration
